text.brief: On September 13, 2000, Judge James Parker apologized from the bench to Wen Ho Lee for the way the government had held him.
text.record: Lee, a Los Alamos scientist born in Taiwan, had spent 278 days in solitary confinement after investigators named him in the search for a leak of W88 warhead data ([Report on Oversight of the Wen Ho Lee Case (Senate Subcommittee, 2001; FAS mirror)](https://irp.fas.org/congress/2001_rpt/whl.html)). Prosecutors charged him with 59 counts of mishandling classified files and never charged him with espionage ([Report on Oversight of the Wen Ho Lee Case (Senate, FAS mirror)](https://irp.fas.org/congress/2001_rpt/whl.html); [Testimony of Attorney General Janet Reno on the Wen Ho Lee case (FAS mirror)](https://sgp.fas.org/congress/2000/reno.html)). He pleaded guilty to one count and went free that day. In 2006 the government and five news organizations paid him about $1.6 million to settle his privacy suit ([Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press: Settlement reached in Lee case (non-profit)](https://www.rcfp.org/settlement-reached-lee-case-involving-reporters-subpoenas/); [The Seattle Times: U.S., 5 news organizations settle Wen Ho Lee's lawsuit (June 3, 2006; media only)](https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20060603/wenholee03/us-5-news-organizations-settle-wen-ho-lees-lawsuit)).
text.reading: The investigation narrowed to one man before it tested the evidence, and the W88 question has never reached a public answer. A defender who picks suspects by origin hands the Party a recruiting argument and leaves the real leak unfound.
text.gapText: Architecture Principles. The judge who freed Lee said the government had embarrassed the nation, and no principle had stopped the case before it reached him.
text.fix: Test every counterintelligence lead against the evidence before naming anyone, and keep ancestry off the suspect list.
